Where: "Creativity is child's play", Robinson paragraph (the 98/10/2 percent figures and footnote 7)
Current text: In fact, data shows how as children get older they lose their ability to think divergently (see Chapter 2), which is a key component of creativity: 98 percent of three- to five-year-olds tested showed they could think in divergent ways, but by the time they were 13 to 15 years old, only 10 percent could think in this way. And when the test was used with 25-year-olds, only 2 percent could think divergently.
Proposed text: Coming up with lots of different answers to one question is called divergent thinking (see Chapter 2), and it is a key part of creativity. The data backs Robinson up, at least in part. Psychologist Kyung Hee Kim analysed nearly 300,000 scores on the Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking, collected between 1968 and 2008. Since 1990, while IQ scores rose, creative thinking scores fell, and the steepest drop was among the youngest children, from kindergarten to third grade. Kim is careful not to say what caused it.
Why: The 98/10/2 figures come from a 1960s study that, as far as we can tell, was never published in a peer-reviewed journal and is retold differently in different places (ages 3-5 or 4-5). Kim's analysis is published, much larger and more recent. New footnote 7 would cite Kim (2011).
Evidence / source: Kim (2011), analysis of about 300,000 Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking scores, 1968-2008 (William & Mary news release, wm.edu/news/stories/2011/smart-yes-creative-not-so-much.php). Journal details to verify.

Where: After "Saying creativity is child's play..." section, as a boxed exercise
Proposed text: TRY IT: YES, AND. Improvisers have one golden rule: accept what your partner says, then add to it. In 2013 researchers at the University of Hertfordshire found that people who did a short improvisation task scored higher on a standard test of divergent thinking (fluency, originality and flexibility) than people who did a control task. It was a small, early study, so treat it as a promising nudge, not proof. Time: 5 minutes. Group: 2 or more. Materials: none. 1. Pair up and pick a silly starting idea, such as "Let's open a restaurant on the moon." 2. Take turns. Every sentence must start with "Yes, and..." and add something new. 3. No "but", no "no". Keep going for three minutes. 4. Stop and write down the five best things you came up with. Use it as a warm-up before any brainstorm.
Why: The chapter is about play but has no exercise to play with. This one needs no materials and has a research basis.
Evidence / source: Lewis & Lovatt (2013), Thinking Skills and Creativity 9, 46-58, University of Hertfordshire. Two experiments (verbal and music improvisation) raised fluency, originality and flexibility on the Alternative Uses Task versus a control task. Early, small-scale evidence; a 2018 review found little evidence for wider improv benefits.

Psychologists have used this test, called the Alternative Uses Task, since the 1960s. Take the full version in the Creativity Test on our site: [site address].

Where: After "So the rubbish bins of corporations everywhere..." (end of the Pyramid section, before the closing summary)
Proposed text: TRY IT: THE PREMORTEM. Naysayers do most damage when they speak last. Psychologist Gary Klein's answer is to invite them in first. Before you pitch an idea, gather the team and say: "It is a year from now. The idea has failed spectacularly. Why?" Everyone writes down reasons in silence for three minutes, then reads them out. Klein described the method in Harvard Business Review in 2007. It builds on 1989 research suggesting that imagining an event has already happened helps people come up with more reasons for it, about 30 percent more in that study. Now the critics are part of the plan instead of the pyramid. Time: 15 minutes. Group: 4 or more. Materials: sticky notes and pens.
Why: Turns the Pyramid of the Powerless into something readers can use on Monday.
Evidence / source: Klein, "Performing a Project Premortem", Harvard Business Review, September 2007; Mitchell, Russo & Pennington (1989) on prospective hindsight (about 30% more reasons generated; check the primary paper).
Confidence: Medium (check the 1989 figure in the original paper)

Current text: For instance, take Thomas Edison's incandescent electric light, an idea he patented in 1879. (Actually, the first incandescent light source was developed by Humphry Davy in 1809.) It became the first 'arch lamp', which then became abbreviated to 'arc lamp' when the marketers got a hold of the idea. Attempts to roll out arc lamps commercially weren't successful because of the lack of a constant supply of electricity. It wasn't until Edison developed a system to supply electricity all over the place that the incandescent light became practical on a large scale. Proposed text: For instance, take Thomas Edison's incandescent electric light, an idea he patented in 1879. (Actually, inventors had been making electric light for decades. Humphry Davy made a strip of platinum glow in 1802 and a few years later showed off a dazzling arc light at the Royal Institution.) Early electric lights never caught on, because nobody could supply a steady, affordable flow of electricity. It wasn't until Edison developed a whole system for delivering power that the incandescent light became practical on a large scale. The point is, Davy's invention wasn't that useful until Edison found a way to make it so.
Why: The 2010 text says the first incandescent light was Davy's in 1809 and that "arch lamp" became "arc lamp" through marketers. Davy's incandescence demo was 1802 and his arc lamp 1808-09 (sources differ); we found no source for the "arch lamp" story, so it is cut.
Evidence / source: Houston Engines of Our Ingenuity; Guinness World Records (arc lamp, Royal Institution, 1808); Open University. Sources disagree on 1808 or 1809 for the arc lamp; 1802 for the platinum strip. The "arch lamp became arc lamp" claim was not found in any source.
Confidence: Medium (arc lamp year differs by source; Edison patent dates not confirmed in this run)
